title: Developing countries may owe more in climate loan repayments than receive by 2036
content:
A new study by CARE Denmark and the CARE Climate Justice Center has revealed that developing countries may soon owe more in climate‑loan repayments than they receive in fresh lending. The researchers analysed roughly 17,500 climate‑loan records reported by developed countries and multilateral lenders from 2011 to 2024, describing the work as the first of its kind to map repayment schedules for this sector.

The analysis shows that repayments on public climate loans, including interest and fees, have nearly tripled in recent years. In 2020 the total was $6.9 billion; by 2024 it had risen to $20.1 billion, which represents about one‑fifth of the public climate finance that developed countries reported providing that year. The researchers project that if climate lending remains at the 2024 level and on the same terms, annual repayments on old and new loans will surpass fresh lending in 2036.

“By not making the backflows of climate finance visible, Global North countries cheat their public,” said John Nordbo, senior climate adviser at CARE Denmark, to Climate Home News. “They give an impression that they are actually more supportive than they are.” The World Bank is the largest lender in the portfolio, followed by Japan and France. Loans worth $489 billion are estimated to cost borrowers $663 billion over their lifetimes.

The findings come as climate finance is set to become a central issue at COP31. Developing nations have secured a new work programme on climate finance for the summit’s agenda, but a key question remains: how will rich countries deliver the agreed $300 billion a year by 2035 amid shrinking aid budgets and spending redirected to other priorities, including defence?

Debt pressures on the Global South are already tightening. Developing countries paid a record $1.4 trillion in principal and interest in 2025, a fifth consecutive annual increase, according to the World Bank’s International Debt Report. Almost 94 % of the most climate‑vulnerable countries are in or at significant risk of debt distress, and they spend nearly 25 times more on debt repayments than on climate action, a September ActionAid report noted. CARE argues that while concessional loans can be appropriate for revenue‑generating climate projects, they are ill‑suited for adaptation measures that protect lives or for countries already in debt distress.
summary: Developing countries may owe more in climate loan repayments than receive by 2036.
author: Climate Home News

title: 91 Leaders Meet at Cop31 in Turkey Amid Doubts Over Climate Action Progress
content: In today’s newsletter: As global leaders gather in Turkey for the UN climate summit, both doubts and hope surround what the annual talks can achieve Good morning. After another year of unprecedented droughts, floods and wildfires driven by human-caused global heating, 91 heads of government will meet tomorrow in Turkey to discuss the climate crisis. They will do so against a backdrop of global instability and conflict. But as high-ranking officials and civil society campaigners settle in for a fortnight of speeches, protests and labyrinthine negotiations at the UN’s 31st annual climate conference, Cop31, many are asking what the point is. UK | Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Monday after a judge praised his victims’ bravery and accused him of living “unhindered by the rules by which decent people live”. US | Donald Trump, Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls have expressed their support for embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, as the head of the world’s most valuable chip company faces an internal investigation over a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Russia | US officials said they would seek a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine, beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday in the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February. Technology | Palantir lobbied a health minister to consider extending its AI technology into GP records, stretching its reach into the NHS in a way doctors fear could undermine trust with patients. Climate | Soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged people to look beyond fossil fuels, leading to an easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.
summary: Global leaders are gathering in Turkey for the UN's 31st annual climate conference to discuss the crisis following a year of extreme weather events. The summit takes place against a backdrop of global instability, with many questioning the effectiveness of the annual talks.

content:
The transition to parenthood can leave fathers and partners’ mental health overlooked, yet data show that depression and anxiety are twice as common among expecting and new fathers compared with global estimates for men.  

Dr. Sharin Baldwin, conducting research at the Centre for Health Services Studies (CHSS), is compiling evidence to better support fathers’ mental health and to inform national research on family health and well‑being.

title: Single-tick experiments reveal rapid Gulf Coast tick bacterial transmission
content: Single‑tick experiments show that bacteria from the Gulf Coast tick can be transmitted to a host within one hour of attachment, before spreading rapidly to lymph nodes and internal tissues. The study, conducted by a recent graduate of the Frederick P. Whiddon College of Medicine, highlights shifting immune defenses during the earliest stages of bacterial infection.
summary: Bacteria from the Gulf Coast tick can be transmitted to its host within one hour of attachment. The bacteria then spread rapidly to lymph nodes and internal tissues, as shown in new research by a recent graduate of the Frederick P. Whiddon College of Medicine.

title: Semaglutide may lower fetal oxygen levels, sheep study suggests
content: Semaglutide, the active ingredient in blockbuster weight‑loss drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy, has been shown in a sheep study to lower fetal oxygen levels. The study suggests a potential risk to unborn babies when the medication is taken during pregnancy. While Ozempic and Wegovy help millions of people lose weight and may improve women’s chances of becoming pregnant, the impact on fetal health if the drugs are continued during pregnancy remains unclear.
summary: Semaglutide, marketed as Ozempic and Wegovy, is a blockbuster weight‑loss drug that helps millions of people lose weight. A sheep study suggests it may lower fetal oxygen levels, raising questions about its safety for pregnant women who continue taking the medication.

title: Immune proteins linked to lower prostate cancer risk
content: A new study led by researchers at Oxford Population Health found that higher levels of proteins that activate and coordinate the immune system are linked to a lower risk of developing prostate cancer. The research suggests that the body’s ability to recognize and respond to abnormal cells may play a key role in the early stages of the disease. These findings could point to new approaches for preventing prostate cancer by targeting immune‑system proteins.
summary: Immune proteins linked to lower prostate cancer risk.

title: PMDD Has Three Distinct Subtypes, Study Finds
content:
Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is a common mood disorder associated with the menstrual cycle.  

A new study published in Nature Communications shows that PMDD does not follow any universal pattern and that there are three subtypes with different patterns of symptoms. The authors hope that this discovery will lead to more individualized treatment.
summary: A study in Nature Communications found that premenstrual dysphoric disorder does not follow a universal pattern but instead has three subtypes with differing symptom patterns. The researchers hope the discovery will lead to more individualized treatment.

title: Hoag researchers detect blood RNA signal that identifies STIC, an ovarian cancer precursor
content:
Hoag researchers have identified a blood‑based RNA signal that can detect serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC), an early precancerous stage of high‑grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC).  

This discovery is significant because ovarian cancer is frequently diagnosed only after the disease has progressed to an advanced, spread‑out stage.
summary: Hoag researchers discovered a molecular warning signal in the blood that identifies serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC). The advance is significant because ovarian cancer is often diagnosed at an advanced stage after the disease has already spread.

title: California voters reject Prop 40 one-time billionaire wealth tax
content: Campaign over Prop 40, as measure was known, was most expensive in state history, flush with Silicon Valley dollars California billionaires won a contentious ballot measure campaign, defeating a proposed one-time tax on their wealth. The bruising campaign over Proposition 40 was the most expensive in state history and witness to back-and-forth dealing from tech billionaires and democratic leaders, including Gavin Newsom, the governor, who steadfastly opposed the measure. While supporters of Prop 40 cast it as a solution to drastic healthcare cuts from Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, opponents led by prosperous billionaires mounted an influential campaign saying the billionaire tax was instead “an everyone tax”.
summary: California voters rejected Proposition 40, a proposed one-time tax on billionaires’ wealth. The campaign, the most expensive in state history, featured billionaires and Governor Gavin Newsom opposing the measure, while supporters tied it to healthcare cuts from the Trump‑backed One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
author: Guardian Business

title: Methane-eating microbes build electrically conductive nanowires
content:
New research published in Nature Communications reveals that anaerobic methanotrophic archaea (ANME) generate electricity by producing nanowires to transmit the current. This finding builds on earlier work by Radboud University microbiologist Cornelia Welte, who demonstrated four years ago that these methane-consuming microorganisms can convert methane into electricity. The study confirms that the organisms utilize these electrically conductive structures to facilitate this energy transfer.

In addition to identifying the mechanism, Welte and her colleagues successfully cultivated these specific microorganisms in the laboratory. The researchers achieved this by growing the microbes on electrodes, allowing them to maintain the organisms in almost pure form for further study.
summary: Research by Cornelia Welte of Radboud University shows that anaerobic methanotrophic archaea convert methane into electricity by producing nanowires to transmit the charge. The researchers also succeeded in cultivating these specific microorganisms in almost pure form in the lab.
author: Phys.org

title: Starling numbers declining, investigating changes in murmurations
content: Starling murmurations, characterized by thousands of birds moving in synchronized waves, continue to draw spectators to city centers and wetlands each autumn. While these displays feature shifting shapes that appear and dissolve rapidly, starling populations are currently declining. Researchers are investigating whether these spectacular aerial displays are also changing in response to the population drop.
summary: Starling numbers are declining, prompting investigation into whether their murmurations are changing. In autumn, starling murmurations attract crowds, with thousands of birds forming waves and shapes in the sky.
author: Phys.org

title: Study identifies single amino acid change that alters Andes virus protein behavior in human cells
content: Mount Sinai researchers identified a single amino acid difference between rodent- and human-derived Andes virus isolates. This specific change alters the behavior of a key viral protein within human cells. The findings help explain biological differences between these closely related virus isolates.
summary: Mount Sinai researchers identified a single amino acid difference between rodent- and human-derived Andes virus isolates that changes how a key viral protein behaves inside human cells. The findings help explain biological differences between closely related virus isolates.
author: Phys.org

title: Math Anxiety May Stop Students From Learning Useful AI and Data Skills
content: Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into daily life and work, capable of generating information, summarizing evidence, and performing calculations. Despite these capabilities, AI does not eliminate the requirement for critical thinking and conceptual understanding.
summary: Math anxiety may be preventing students from acquiring useful AI and data skills. Artificial intelligence can generate information, summarize evidence, and perform calculations, but it still requires critical thinking and conceptual understanding.
author: Phys.org

title: Global carbon pollution falls slightly, linked to Iran war oil shocks, study says
content: A new study reports that global carbon pollution dropped slightly this year. Scientists attribute the decline to oil shocks from the Iran war rather than progress in energy and climate action.
summary: Global carbon pollution dropped slightly this year. Scientists attribute the decline to oil shocks from the Iran war rather than climate action, according to a new study.
author: Phys.org

title: Digging up the past can change the ground beneath it
content:
Archaeological digs uncover historical layers while simultaneously altering the very landscapes that have protected them for centuries. Excavation can modify local water flow, increase soil erosion, and destabilize exposed remains, reshaping the site’s physical context.

Researchers from Istanbul Technical University and the U. S. have demonstrated how computer models can help archaeologists anticipate and manage these changes, with a particular focus on erosion risks. In a case study of an Early Bronze Age settlement in Türkiye, the team reconstructed the terrain both before and after excavation to illustrate the impacts and guide future preservation efforts.
summary: Archaeological excavation uncovers the past but also changes the landscape that has preserved sites for centuries or millennia. These changes influence water flow, soil erosion and the stability of exposed remains.
author: Phys.org

title: Ice cores reveal early 1900s Anaconda Copper Mine pollution spread to Arctic
content: Ice core records have revealed extensive air pollution linked to early‑20th‑century copper production. The Anaconda Copper Mine complex near Butte, Montana, emitted large amounts of particulate matter, including arsenic and other heavy metals. Wind transported these particles across the Arctic, where storms eventually deposited them on the ground, where they became part of the ice layers now studied by scientists.
summary: About a century ago, the Anaconda Copper Mine complex near Butte, Montana, emitted vast amounts of air pollution. Arsenic and other heavy‑metal particles were carried by winds to the Arctic, where storms deposited them onto ice layers.
author: Phys.org

title: Richard Robson's 1974 experiments create foundation for metal‑organic frameworks
content:
The piece discusses efforts to make metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) easier to shape for use in electronic devices.  

The background of MOFs traces to 1974, when University of Melbourne chemistry professor Richard Robson proposed replacing the wooden balls and metal rods of structural models with molecules and chemical bonds. He experimented with copper ions linked by a four‑armed organic molecule, creating a structure with a cavity that laid the foundation for MOFs—a class of porous materials formed by linking metal ions with organic molecules. Their pores can capture pollutants, support chemical reactions and store gases, giving MOFs a wide range of potential applications.
summary: In 1974, University of Melbourne chemistry professor Richard Robson began experimenting with copper ions linked by a four‑armed organic molecule, creating a cavity‑containing structure. His work established the basis for metal‑organic frameworks, porous materials that can capture pollutants, support reactions and store gases.
author: Phys.org

title: Neutrino discoveries could reveal secrets of the galaxy’s centre, says columnist
content: Columnist Chanda Prescod‑Weinstein says that understanding neutrinos is among the most pressing scientific issues in physics. In her column she highlights recent neutrino discoveries that she finds exciting and notes that these findings could provide new insights into the centre of our galaxy.
summary: Columnist Chanda Prescod-Weinstein says understanding neutrinos is one of the most pressing scientific issues in physics. She notes that recent neutrino discoveries could provide new insights into the galactic centre.
author: New Scientist

title: New Chinese “web-loving bug” may spend its whole life on a spider’s web
content: A species of “web-loving bug” from China lives on a spider's web and seems to follow its arachnid host around. The insect may be too small for the spider to bother attacking
summary: A newly described species of “web-loving bug” from China lives on a spider’s web and seems to follow its arachnid host. The insect may be too small for the spider to bother attacking.
