title: Study Reveals Ga and Fante Held Over 70% of Ghanaian Civil Service Jobs in 1950s
content: It was a landmark in history: In 1957, Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African state to achieve independence from colonial rule, having previously been under the control of Great Britain. But gaining political independence does not mean the past is left behind, and there has long been public debate about the many long-term effects of the colonial period on state and society in subsequent decades. Now, an empirically rich study explores one aspect of the Ghanaian state, the composition of its bureaucracy, during and after British rule. The study finds that two ethnic groups, the Ga and the Fante, which made up 14 percent of the population combined, held over 70 percent of public-sector positions in the 1950s, suggesting goods such as desirable jobs had been heavily distributed along group lines. “At the moment of independence, you have a state that is not meritocratic, and is highly captured by certain ethnic groups,” says MIT scholar Noah Nathan, co-author of a newly published paper detailing the study’s findings. As a result, he adds, “You can imagine the politics that creates, which are demands to equalize access to state power and state authority. And things start off on this foot of ethnic political competition over the state. That is in part a legacy of colonial state-building.” At least in this case, “Independence in Africa wasn’t this hard break from the past,” suggests Nathan, a Ford International Professor of Political Science in MIT’s Department of Political Science. “Africans became the leaders of their countries, but the state institutions that they inherited weren’t born fresh at independence. They were carried over from the colonial period.” The paper, “ The Seeds of State Capture: Merit and Patrimonialism in the Colonial Bureaucracy,” is published in advance online form in the American Political Science Review. Nathan’s co-authors are Sarah Brierley, an associate professor at the London School of Economics and Political Science; George Kwaku Ofoso, an associate professor at the London School of Economics and Political Science; and Tingxuan Zhu PhD ’26, a recent graduate of MIT’s doctoral program in political science at MIT. Analyzing names To conduct the study, the scholars dug into records from the period of British rule in Ghana, which extended from the 19th century until 1957. Using documents from the British National Archives, they examined individual-level employment records for 11,702 bureaucrats from the colonial-era civil service, building a dataset spanning from 1897 to 1955. The records included 6,879 Ghanaian civil servants and 4,805 European civil servants. The scholars’ aim was to shed light on the dynamics of civil service hiring and politics. British leaders at the time, and some commentators subsequently, have cast the colonial state as one built on rational, merit-based principles — what scholars call a “Weberian” bureaucracy, named after the famous German sociologist Max Weber. Scholars say that other types of bureaucracies, in contrast, display “patrimonialism,” with jobs being assigned not on merit but through patronage. To analyze this question further, the scholars looked at 13.8 million names of registered voters from contemporary Ghana, along with localized ethnicity data from the 2010 national census. They used this to establish a baseline of the relationship between names and ethnicity in the country. Then, the scholars went back to the historical archives, and, using the names there, determined the ethnicities of past Ghanaian civil servants, from 1897 to 1955. Ultimately this approach showed that on the eve of independence, the Ga and Fante had managed to gain a percentage of civil service jobs that was five times greater than the percentage of the population they represented. That strongly suggests that the colonial-era bureaucracy built under British rule was not merit-based, at least in terms of overall composition. “Scholars have said this post-1957 independent Ghana brings with it the introduction of patrimonialism into the bureaucracy, and we’re saying this was going on long before,” Nathan explains. “It actually wasn’t meritocratic at all, and Kwame Nkrumah, the first president of Ghana, didn’t inherit some Weberian rational bureaucracy that he then destroyed. He inherited this thing rife with patrimonialism and patronage, that he then adapted. And that’s a very different interpretation of the post-independence period.” Exams and education To further examine the question of merit, the scholars even obtained individual-level results from Ghana’s civil service exams, then analyzed those in relation to which applicants got hired — or passed over for jobs. The results indicate little correspondence between exam results and job offers, again suggesting that ethnicity and social ties mattered more in hiring, on aggregate. “If you were from the right ethnic group, you were going to get a job, even if you did pretty poorly on the civil service exam,” Nathan says. “And people from disfavored ethnic groups who did much better on the exam were not getting the same positions.” The study also rules out a seemingly logical explanation for at least part of the ethnic skew in the composition of the Ghanaian civil service — that hiring reflected levels of educational attainment, even if access to schooling itself might have reflected ethnic iniquities. But the data indicate that was not a factor. The scholars located every school in the country geographically, dating to the 1890s, and closely measured access to education for all ethnic groups over time. The Ga and Fante groups may have had some initial advantages in this regard, but by the 1930s, many other groups had caught up in educational attainment and still were not procuring the same relative numbers of civil services jobs through the 1950s. “At least in this case, that can’t explain why these two groups got favored in the hiring process,” Nathan says. “It wasn’t just a direct outcome of the fact that some parts of society had more education than others.” As it happens, geographical proximity to civil service jobs is also not an explanatory factor; the scholars also examined the locations of government offices and found they cannot account for the quantity of jobs going to the Ga and Fante. Out of sight Instead, the researchers believe the likeliest scenario is that, once established in the civil service, people from the Ga and Fante managed to use their social connections to get more and more jobs offered to others from their own groups. Moreover, they may have done so not necessarily with explicit British approval, but with something more resembling indifference on the part of the colonial rulers. “The mechanics of the hiring process were very decentralized,” Nathan says. “And the British didn’t know very much about the society they were governing. That created an information asymmetry where local bureaucrats could get friends into jobs in a way their superiors were either not aware of or didn’t have very much incentive to stop.” All told, Nathan observes, “The ministry of finance in Ghana in 1957 isn’t some new thing that’s created from scratch. It’s the colonial ministry of finance that’s been in place for 60 years, and the bureaucrats in it showed up to work the next day in the same jobs. [The new leaders] inherited thousands of employees who had gotten there through this process.” The study is one of several that Nathan has published using data to answer questions that span both political science and history. Quantifying the issue in a granular way helps illuminate the large-scale political dynamics. “People have written about this in broad strokes, even the fact that certain ethnic groups in some countries got more access to positions than others, but they haven’t had detailed microdata on exactly who got which job and when,” Nathan says. “That’s the innovation of our paper … we could unpack the nuts and bolts of how this hiring process happened, and in doing so dispel some conventional wisdom about how African states were built in the colonial period.” The new paper is not the only piece of scholarship taking this kind of data-intensive approach to studying colonial state-building and its legacy. Ada Johnson-Kanu, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Kentucky, has conducted this sort of study of Nigeria’s bureaucracy over time, in work she completed in 2021. Nathan, for his part, says he hopes that other scholars can expand upon this kind of data-driven approach to digging into certain historical questions. “There is just incredibly rich archival evidence out there in the world for a lot of countries,” Nathan observes. “I think this is a really fun way to do research.”
summary: The study examined 11,702 colonial-era Ghanaian civil servants and found that the Ga and Fante, who made up 14% of the population, held over 70% of public‑sector positions in the 1950s. The analysis also showed little correspondence between civil service exam results and job offers, indicating ethnicity and social ties mattered more than merit.
author: MIT News

title: Podcast: Professor Russell Foster discusses seasonal affective disorder and remedies
content:
A new Guardian science podcast explores the reality of winter‑time depression. The episode notes that while many people feel low as nights lengthen, a smaller group can develop a more severe condition known since the 1980s as seasonal affective disorder (SAD), which can be debilitating.

In the programme, journalist Ian Sample interviews Professor Russell Foster, a circadian neuroscience specialist at the University of Oxford. Foster discusses current scientific ideas about the mechanisms behind SAD and reviews the evidence concerning the most effective ways to address the disorder.

Listeners are reminded of crisis support options: Samaritans in the UK and Ireland (freephone 116 123), the US 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call, text or chat at 988lifeline.org), Australia’s Lifeline (13 11 14), and additional international helplines via befrienders.org. The Guardian’s science podcast can be supported at theguardian.com/sciencepod.
summary: Ian Sample speaks with Russell Foster, a professor of circadian neuroscience at the University of Oxford, about seasonal affective disorder (SAD). Foster explains the hypothesized mechanism of the condition and reviews evidence on the best ways to treat it.
author: Guardian Science

title: Valley Fog Clears by Afternoon Over Appalachian Plateau, Nov 8 2026
content:
NASA’s Earth Observatory released a paired satellite view of the Appalachian Plateau and the Cumberland River on November 8, 2026, illustrating the rapid disappearance of valley fog from morning to afternoon. The left‑hand image, captured in natural color by the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) aboard NASA’s Terra satellite, shows white low clouds filling the branching river valleys amid brown and green autumn terrain. The right‑hand image, taken later that day in false color by the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) on NOAA‑21, depicts clear skies with dark‑blue rivers and lakes winding through bright‑green vegetation.

The morning fog, described by the article as a type of cloud that forms near the ground, is typical for the region in late autumn. As nights lengthen, the ground radiates heat, cooling the air just above it to the dew point where water vapor condenses into tiny droplets. Because cold air is denser, it flows downslope and pools in valleys, producing the observed fog. The imagery highlights fog accumulation across eastern Kentucky and southwestern West Virginia, as well as along the Cumberland River and its reservoirs in north‑central Tennessee and south‑central Kentucky, where rivers add moisture to the valley air.

According to the National Weather Service, temperatures at many locations on the morning of November 8 dipped into the 30s °F before giving way to a mild, sunny afternoon. Forecasters reported locally dense valley fog that morning, and earlier in the week dense fog had covered a broader area, prompting advisories for hazardous travel conditions.

The images were generated from MODIS data accessed through NASA’s EOSDIS LANCE and GIBS/Worldview services, and from VIIRS data accessed through the same NASA portals and the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS). The story accompanying the imagery was written by Kathryn Hansen, with photography credited to Lauren Dauphin. Downloads of the Terra MODIS and NOAA‑20 VIIRS JPEG files are available for the November 8, 2026 observations.
summary: Valley Fog Clears by Afternoon Over Appalachian Plateau, Nov 8 2026.
author: NASA News

title: APOD November 10, 2026 – Saturn behind Moon captured from Sardinia
content:
The Astronomy Picture of the Day for November 10, 2026 features a digital composite that captures Saturn as it is briefly hidden behind Earth’s Moon.  The image combines three separate photographs taken from Sardinia, Italy, after sunset: one of Saturn before the occultation and two of the Moon taken with different exposure lengths.  A bright point near the planet is identified as the star 85 Aquarii, which lies farther behind Saturn than the Moon does.

The accompanying explanation notes that Saturn does not actually vanish; it is simply obscured when the Moon passes in front of it, an event known as an occultation.  A similar Saturn‑Moon occultation was visible in early 2025 for observers along a narrow corridor that stretched from Greenland through central Europe to northern Africa.  According to the entry, the next time the Moon will move in front of Saturn for any location on Earth will not occur until 2031.

The picture is credited to Roberto Ortu, with the APOD entry edited by Robert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, and Keighley Rockcliffe.  The service is provided by the Astronomy Picture of the Day program, a collaboration between the NASA Goddard Space Flight Center’s Astrophysics Science Division and Michigan Technological University.  A preview notes that tomorrow’s APOD will feature a “small but mighty” image.
summary: The Astronomy Picture of the Day for November 10, 2026 shows Saturn hidden by the Moon in an occultation, using a digital fusion of three images taken from Sardinia, Italy after sunset. The bright dot near Saturn is the star 85 Aquarii, and the next visible Moon‑Saturn occultation will occur in 2031.
author: NASA News

title: Show HN: Open‑source MeowDisplay lets iPhone mirror Mac screen in reverse
content: Hey HN and Cats, thank you for checking this out! Github: https://github. Com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay EDIT 2: I should've mentioned that MeowDisplay started as a fork of OpenDisplay: https://github. Com/peetzweg/opendisplay which provided the foundational screen capture, virtual display, encoding and iPhone/iPad receivers. I've since taken it in a more phone-first direction, with work on the interaction, streaming and security layers. I've credited OpenDisplay and its developer Philip in the README under "Built on OpenDisplay". MeowDisplay is my take on the control your Mac from your phone scene. Available on iPhones, iPads and Macs, with Android rn in closed testing. The website has interactive illustrative demos if you'd like to see the app demonstrated. I think MeowDisplay does a few things differently, some of which I prefer and you might too. Such as Window view: allowing multiple tabs in split-screen type panes. Traditional Mirror/Extend views exist as alternatives. Floating windows: coming in the 2.1 release. Touch input approaches: Direct Touch(Classic or Natural), experimental Smart Touch, and Trackpad mode alongside Apple Pencil support. Doesn't sacrifice display space for a trackpad, use all of the phone's screen with your preferred mode. Stage Peek: shows a scrollable and searchable list of your Mac's windows on your phone along with an app drawer when you hold and pull on the left edge of your screen. It's free and open source so you can try it and see if it's for you without having to commit to it or anything. EDIT: I've used MeowDisplay during development whilst I was travelling between cities, left my acbook at home clamshell, powered, external display attached, and used it for small tasks remotely, it was pretty reliable even on a 5G network on a moving bus. Meow, Jai Comments URL: https://news. Ycombinator. Com/item? Id=50429636 Points: 107 # Comments: 38
summary: MeowDisplay is an open‑source app that lets users control a Mac from an iPhone or iPad, acting as reverse mirroring. It began as a fork of OpenDisplay, runs on iOS and macOS with Android in closed testing, and offers split‑screen windows, multiple touch input modes and a Stage Peek window list.
author: Hacker News

title: Google DeepMind AI tool formally verifies Signal Protocol security
content: DeepMind researchers have used a new AI tool to formally verify that the Signal encryption protocol functions as intended. The team described this achievement as a step toward a broader ambition: applying similar formal verification methods to “all the software of the world.”
summary: DeepMind researchers formally verified that the widely used encryption protocol works as intended. Their stretch goal is to do the same for “all the software of the world.”
author: Wired

title: Meta expands Instagram AI age‑guessing tool worldwide
content: Meta announced that it will roll out Instagram’s AI‑driven age‑guessing system on a global scale. The technology will analyze clues to identify users it suspects are teenagers, even when those users provide an adult birthdate.
summary: Meta will roll out Instagram’s AI age‑guessing technology globally. The AI will search for clues indicating users may be teenagers even when they provide an adult birthday.
author: TechCrunch

title: California voters reject Proposition 40 one-time 5% billionaire tax
content: California voters rejected Proposition 40, a one‑time 5 % tax on billionaires, according to an AP report on Monday. Tech leaders spent roughly ten times as much as the tax’s supporters to defeat the measure, and founders and economists interviewed by TechCrunch before the vote were divided on whether the tax would have driven wealthy residents away or merely reduced their fortunes.
summary: California voters rejected Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on billionaires, the AP reported Monday. Tech leaders outspent backers roughly 10 to 1 to defeat it, and founders and economists interviewed by TechCrunch were split on whether it would have driven out wealthy residents or just trimmed their fortunes.
author: TechCrunch

title: Apple redesigns MacBook Pro with OLED touchscreen, starts at £2,899
content:
Apple has refreshed its flagship MacBook Pro for the first time in five years, making the notebook slightly slimmer and noticeably lighter. The redesign introduces a new PROLED XDR OLED display that includes the first touchscreen ever seen on a Mac, and the models are offered in 14‑inch and 16‑inch sizes. Rather than replacing the existing lineup, the OLED versions sit alongside the standard MacBook Pro as a higher‑priced alternative.

The OLED MacBook Pro is marketed with “fantastic” display quality and “killer” performance, but it carries a premium price. Base models start at £2,899 (€3,299/$2,899/A$4,599), roughly £400 more than comparable LCD‑spec machines, a cost increase attributed in part to higher RAM expenses. The devices are positioned as serious work machines with a correspondingly serious price tag.
summary: Apple has redesigned its flagship MacBook Pro for the first time in five years, making it slimmer, lighter and adding a PROLED XDR OLED touchscreen display. The new 14‑inch and 16‑inch models start at £2,899, about £400 more than comparable LCD versions, reflecting higher costs including RAM upgrades.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Best under‑desk walking pads tested for comfort, noise and storage
content:
An expert has evaluated a selection of walking pads, assessing each model for comfort, noise level and ease of storage. The review is positioned as a guide for people who want to increase their daily steps while working at a desk or watching television, and it compares the under‑desk treadmills to larger, conventional running treadmills, noting that walking pads are generally lighter, smaller and simpler to store.

The article also references the NHS recommendation that a modest goal of ten minutes of brisk walking each day can introduce moderate‑intensity activity and lower the risk of early death by up to fifteen percent. By highlighting the convenience of walking pads for those with busy schedules or desk‑bound jobs, the piece suggests they may help users incorporate the recommended activity without the space and handling challenges of traditional treadmills.
summary: Best under‑desk walking pads tested for comfort, noise and storage.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Australia to create AI safety regulator and mandatory reporting after OpenAI breach
content: Australia's prime minister said its government would set up a new AI safety regulator and Labor would consider six key obligations on AI companies. The review made 18 recommendations. Anthony Albanese said: 'We accept all of the recommendations, and we’ve commenced work to implement them.' Australia to introduce mandatory reporting after OpenAI hack to combat artificial intelligence ‘going rogue’
summary: Australia's prime minister announced the government will set up a new AI safety regulator and that Labor will consider six key obligations for AI companies. The plan includes mandatory reporting after an OpenAI hack and follows a review with 18 recommendations that the prime minister said have been accepted for implementation.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang sued by shareholders over alleged Chinese spy affair
content: Nvidia and its chief executive Jensen Huang are facing a shareholder lawsuit that accuses them of defrauding investors in connection with a Chinese‑spying scandal involving the $4.3 trillion (≈£3.2 trillion) company. The legal action was reported alongside comments from former President Donald Trump, who said the FBI is investigating Huang’s alleged affair with a Chinese spy. Business‑focused commentary has noted that the controversy may prompt Nvidia’s board to consider succession planning.
summary: Nvidia and its chief executive Jensen Huang have been sued by shareholders accusing them of defrauding investors in a Chinese spying scandal. The lawsuit was filed as Donald Trump said the FBI is investigating Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Nvidia boss Huang under investigation for alleged Chinese spy affair
content: Faisal Islam reports that Nvidia chief Jensen Huang is currently under investigation for an alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Islam characterizes Huang as significantly more consequential to the future world order than other technology executives.
summary: Huang, the boss of US tech giant Nvidia, is being investigated over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. He is described as far more important to the future of the world order than other tech bosses.
author: BBC Technology

title: California voters reject one-off billionaire wealth tax, US media predicted
content: California voters rejected a one‑off billionaire wealth tax, a result that US media had predicted. The measure was described as a key test for the global campaign against inequality, but warnings that the super‑rich would leave the state prevailed.
summary: California voters rejected a one-off billionaire wealth tax, a result US media had predicted. The measure was seen as a key test for the global campaign against inequality, but warnings that the super‑rich would leave the state won out.
author: Euronews

title: Trump says Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang knew nothing about alleged Chinese spy
content: U.S. President Donald Trump said the FBI is investigating a matter that involves Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang and alleged connections to a Chinese government agent. Trump said he had spoken with Huang, who denied knowing the individual was a spy, and the president voiced confidence in the tech executive.
summary: President Donald Trump said the FBI is investigating a matter involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and alleged links to a Chinese government agent. Trump said he spoke with Huang, who denied knowing the person was a spy, and Trump expressed confidence in the executive.
author: Euronews

title: Senegal migrant boat wreckage shown; 39 people dead
content: At least 39 people have died after a migrant boat sank off Senegal’s Atlantic coast. Footage shows the shattered vessel washed ashore while rescuers continue searching for victims.
summary: At least 39 people have died after a migrant boat sank off Senegal's Atlantic coast. Footage shows the shattered vessel washed ashore while rescuers continue searching for victims.
author: Euronews

title: Trump backs Pete Hegseth as Rep. Thomas Massie moves to impeach him over Iran action
content:
Trump has announced he will support Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth as a Republican lawmaker pushes for an impeachment vote.

Congressman Thomas Massie is seeking to impeach Hegseth, alleging that the secretary has conducted military action against Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization.
summary: President Donald Trump vowed to back Pete Hegseth. Republican Congressman Thomas Massie is seeking to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging military action against Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization.
author: Euronews

title: Trump says Iran war effectively over, Iran denies any planned talks
content: Speaking after meeting Qatar’s prime minister, a key mediator, Trump said further strikes were “quite unlikely” but that the US was “locked and loaded”. Meanwhile, Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei told Washington to stop “manufacturing fake news about imaginary talks”.
summary: Trump says Iran war effectively over, Iran denies any planned talks.
author: Euronews

title: South Africa ANC receives 30.76% in municipal vote, its worst ever
content: The African National Congress, which has dominated South African politics since the end of apartheid, received 30.76 percent of votes in municipal elections, its worst‑ever performance, according to the electoral commission on Sunday. With no party winning outright in many municipalities, the results set the stage for fraught multiparty coalition negotiations to govern several major cities.
summary: The African National Congress took 30.76 percent of votes in South Africa's municipal elections, its worst‑ever electoral performance, the electoral commission said Sunday. The results set the stage for fraught multiparty coalition negotiations to govern several major cities.
author: France 24

title: 200,000 free tickets for schools to attend Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games
content: Dakar 2026 will distribute 200,000 free tickets to schools and community organisations as part of the Youth Olympic Games, aiming to let as many young people as possible experience the event. This initiative is reported by FRANCE 24’s team on the ground.
summary: 200,000 free tickets will be distributed to schools and community organisations for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games. The aim is to give as many young people as possible the chance to experience the Games, FRANCE 24’s team on the ground reports.
author: France 24

title: Chinese business leaders and policymakers attend Web Summit in Lisbon in record delegation
content:
The Web Summit, one of Europe’s largest annual technology conferences, opened in Lisbon this week with the biggest delegation yet of Chinese business leaders and policymakers. The event attracted significant attention from the EU, reflecting the growing importance of China’s tech sector in Europe.

During the opening, FRANCE 24’s Charles Pellegrin spoke with Dr. Dan Wang, China Director at Eurasia Group. Their conversation focused on EU‑China technology relations, the heightened suspicion following the Nvidia spying scandal, and the potential implications of the EU’s pursuit of technology sovereignty for China.
summary: The Web Summit in Lisbon featured the biggest ever delegation of Chinese business leaders and policymakers. France 24's Charles Pellegrin interviewed Dr. Dan Wang, China Director at Eurasia Group, on EU‑China tech relations, the Nvidia spying scandal, and the EU’s tech sovereignty agenda.
author: France 24

title: Russian and Ukrainian officials meet in US‑backed talks, first since February
content: Russian and Ukrainian officials met on Tuesday, November 10, for the first U.S.-brokered talks since February. The meeting followed U.S. President Donald Trump’s statement last week that a broad deal could end the war in Ukraine and secure Europe. FRANCE 24’s correspondent in Kyiv, Emmanuelle Chaze, and International Affairs Editor Rochelle Ferguson report further details.
summary: Russian and Ukrainian officials meet in US‑backed talks, first since February.
author: France 24

title: US Rep. Thomas Massie pushes impeachment vote against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
content:
On Monday, November 9, US Republican Thomas Massie moved to force a vote to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. Massie urged fellow Republicans to remove Hegseth, a prominent Trump‑era official, after sweeping election losses that were partly blamed on fallout from the war in Iran.

FRANCE 24’s Washington correspondent Fraser Jackson reports further details.
summary: On Monday, November 9, US Republican Thomas Massie moved to force a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. He urged fellow Republicans to remove the Trump administration official after sweeping election losses blamed in part on fallout from the war in Iran.
author: France 24

title: Peru Welcomes Pope Leo XIV, Unveils Giant Statue Ahead of Visit
content: On Wednesday, November 11, Pope Leo XIV visited Peru as part of his South American tour, following stops in Uruguay and Argentina. The American‑born pontiff had lived in Peru for several years and became a Peruvian citizen. Ahead of his arrival, Peru unveiled a giant statue in his honour.
summary: Pope Leo XIV visited Peru on Wednesday, November 11, as part of his South American tour following stops in Uruguay and Argentina. Peru unveiled a giant statue in his honour before his arrival, noting that the American‑born pontiff had lived in Peru for several years and became a Peruvian citizen.
author: France 24

title: Greek National Opera lets seniors perform, showing art has no age
content: A recent Greek National Opera production afforded a group of seniors the chance to channel their young-at-heart energy into onstage performances, proving that no one's too old to learn something new. It challenged the premise that retirement means surrendering to a sedentary lifestyle and extinguishing one’s creative spirit.
summary: A recent Greek National Opera production gave a group of seniors the chance to perform onstage. It challenged the idea that retirement requires a sedentary lifestyle and ends creative expression.
author: France 24

title: France vows strong response to October freezer cyberattack blamed on Iran
content:
France’s Foreign Minister, Jean‑Noël Barrot, announced on Tuesday, November 10, that Paris will take decisive action in response to a major cyberattack that targeted hundreds of supermarket fridges in October. The French government has blamed the attack on Iran.

Barrot told France Info that the purpose of the response is to deter any future attempts, whether from Iran or elsewhere, to repeat the incident.
summary: On Tuesday, November 10, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Paris will not rule out any measures in response to the October cyberattack on hundreds of supermarket fridges that France blames on Iran. He said the goal is to deter anyone, in Iran or elsewhere, from carrying out a similar attack again.
author: France 24

title: African nations intensify fight against fake news amid free‑speech concerns
content: The fight against fake news is gaining momentum across Africa, spanning countries such as Ghana and Mozambique. Efforts to curb disinformation are paired with calls for free‑speech safeguards, a combination that places some governments in an inconvenient position.
summary: The fight against fake news is gaining momentum from Ghana to Mozambique. Combating disinformation also requires safeguards for free speech, leaving some governments in an inconvenient position.
author: DW World

title: Fact check: Fake and AI-manipulated images spread after Krakow mass shooting
content: DW Fact Check reported that, in the hours following the Krakow mass shooting, fake and AI‑manipulated images circulated online, contributing to false narratives about the incident. The fact‑check examined which content was authentic and which was not.
summary: Fake and AI-manipulated images spread online in the hours after the Krakow attack, fueling false narratives about the mass shooting. DW Fact Check examined what was real and what wasn’t.
author: DW World

title: Heavy rains in Gaza cause sand dune collapse, killing infant and three children
content: Heavy rains swept across Gaza over the weekend, triggering a sand‑dune collapse that struck several tents. The UN aid coordination office (OCHA) reported that an infant drowned and five Gazans were killed, including three children, when the dune fell on their shelters.
summary: An infant reportedly drowned and five Gazans were killed, including three children, when a sand dune collapsed on their tents during the first heavy rains that swept across Gaza over the weekend. The UN aid coordination office (OCHA) reported the incident.
author: UN News

title: UN agency says El Niño could cost global economy $11 trillion, threaten food security
content: The United Nations agency that works on rural poverty in developing nations said on Monday that the El Niño extreme‑weather pattern could cost the global economy as much as $11 trillion and pose a serious threat to food security.
summary: The UN agency tackling rural poverty in developing countries said on Monday that the El Niño extreme weather pattern could cost the global economy up to $11 trillion. It warned the phenomenon could seriously impact food security.
author: UN News

title: At least 56 migrants die in weekend shipwrecks off Senegal and Greece
content: At least 56 people died in a series of shipwrecks off Senegal and Greece over the weekend, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) reported on Monday. The IOM described the deaths as a stark reminder of the deadly risks migrants face on the Atlantic and Mediterranean.
summary: At least 56 people died in a series of shipwrecks off Senegal and Greece over the weekend. The International Organization for Migration said on Monday the deaths highlight the deadly risks migrants face on the Atlantic and Mediterranean.
author: UN News

title: EU manufacturers may abandon competition with China by 2030, warns chamber chief
content:
Jens Eskelund, the head of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China, warned that if current trends persist, European manufacturers may abandon efforts to compete with Chinese rivals by the end of the decade, citing concerns about mass job losses. He said Europe might need to permit its companies to integrate into Chinese firms’ supply chains.

Eskelund added that companies operating in China are moving from a “Made in China for China” mindset toward a “Made in China for the world” approach, reflecting a possible shift in strategy if competition proves untenable.
summary: EU manufacturers may abandon competition with China by 2030, warns chamber chief.
author: Guardian World

title: Author Jojo Moyes faces EU travel ban and €10,000 fine over border system glitches
content:
The European Union has sued IBM and two other European firms over its digital entry and exit system (EES), citing errors that have left some British travellers incorrectly flagged as having overstayed the post‑Brexit 90‑day limit.  

Author Jojo Moyes is one of the UK citizens named in the complaint. Because of glitches in the EU’s digital security controls, she is facing a two‑year travel ban and a €10,000 (£8,300) fine. Moyes is among a group of British travellers who say their trips to the EU have not been properly recorded since the EES was introduced.
summary: Author Jojo Moyes faces a two-year EU travel ban and a €10,000 (£8,300) fine due to glitches in the EU’s digital entry and exit system. She is one of several UK travellers who say their trips have not been correctly recorded since the system was introduced.
author: Guardian World

title: Viktor Orbán’s brother detained in people‑smuggling probe, PM says
content:
Hungarian authorities have detained the brother of Prime Minister Viktor Orbán as part of a people‑smuggling investigation, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced. The arrest was carried out by the national asset protection and recovery office (NVVH), the anti‑graft body created to probe alleged corruption from the former prime minister’s 16‑year tenure.

In a statement, the NVVH said it and police detained four individuals and conducted searches of homes in Budapest and Pest county.
summary: Hungarian authorities have detained Viktor Orbán’s brother in a people‑smuggling investigation, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said. The anti‑graft body National Asset Protection and Recovery Office (NVVH) said it and police detained four people and searched homes in Budapest and Pest county.
author: Guardian World

title: US, Russia, Ukraine hold Abu Dhabi talks; Spain police officer killed in Oviedo blast
content:
Talks among the United States, Russia and Ukraine opened in Abu Dhabi, described as the first substantive negotiations in months. The discussions focus on ending a conflict that has lasted more than four years, with U.S. officials saying they seek a “final end” to the Russia‑Ukraine war as the talks begin.

Separately, Spanish authorities reported that a police officer from the canine unit was killed and an explosives‑disposal expert was seriously injured by a backpack explosion in Oviedo. The officers had been sent to an address in the Villafría neighbourhood after a prior alert about a shooting that wounded a 17‑year‑old girl, according to El Mundo.
summary: US, Russia, Ukraine hold Abu Dhabi talks; Spain police officer killed in Oviedo blast.
author: Guardian World

title: NSW inquiry recommends banning Redeemer Baptist School from new enrolments
content:
A New South Wales parliamentary inquiry into Redeemer Baptist School, a private religious school in western Sydney, has recommended that the institution be barred from enrolling new students. The inquiry also called for police investigations into allegations of sexual assault and other forms of abuse reported at the school.

Former students and teachers who appeared before the inquiry described a series of disturbing claims, including sexual, physical, psychological, spiritual and financial abuse. The inquiry’s recommendations focus on preventing further enrolments while law‑enforcement reviews the alleged misconduct.
summary: A New South Wales parliamentary inquiry recommended that police investigate allegations of sexual assault and other abuse at Redeemer Baptist School. The inquiry also advised that the school be barred from enrolling new students after former students and teachers described sexual, physical, psychological, spiritual and financial abuse.
author: Guardian World

title: Mortgage holders' confidence hits lowest since 1994, Westpac survey shows
content:
A Westpac survey shows confidence among households with mortgages has fallen to its lowest point in more than three decades, a level not seen since 1994. The poll also recorded a growing sense of “helplessness” about the economy and a decline in the consumer‑sentiment index for November, taking it to a four‑year low as pessimism about near‑term prospects deepens.

The results come as a sharp shift in financial markets has raised expectations of a Reserve Bank rate cut by this time next year, and Treasury Minister Jim Chalmers is reported to be under increasing pressure to curb spending.
summary: Confidence among mortgaged households has crashed to its lowest level in more than three decades, according to a Westpac survey. The survey also showed the consumer sentiment index fell to a four‑year low in November amid growing helplessness about the economy and expectations of a possible Reserve Bank rate cut by next year.
author: Guardian World

title: Australia to mandate AI incident reporting after OpenAI Medicare data breach
content:
The Australian government announced that it will amend criminal law to require mandatory reporting of artificial‑intelligence incidents after a breach involving OpenAI. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese released the recommendations of a rapid review into the June breach of a Medicare statistics reporting service portal run by Services Australia, while noting that the full findings and report will be published later. The review did not impose criminal penalties on OpenAI for the incident.

The proposed legal changes aim to prevent companies from claiming ignorance of a compromised system. They call for continuous security controls throughout AI development and deployment, systematic risk identification, rapid mandatory notification of incidents to the government, independent model evaluation, and the publication of safety and security frameworks. Companies would also be required to adapt to evolving standards and rules as AI technologies change.
summary: Australia to mandate AI incident reporting after OpenAI Medicare data breach.
author: Guardian World

title: David Jones’s finances were reviewed and restructuring flagged months before it fell into administration
content:
David Jones administrators revealed that the retailer’s finances were reviewed six months before the company entered administration, and that restructuring was discussed three months prior to the filing.

The timing of these reviews has prompted questions about the department store group’s continued purchase of new products and its delayed payments to certain brands, which occurred before the company announced on Thursday that it could not meet its debts.
summary: David Jones’s finances were reviewed and restructuring flagged months before it fell into administration.
author: Guardian World

title: The Odyssey cruise ship seized in Singapore after operator ran out of money
content: The Odyssey was meant to take guests around the world for years, but the trip was cut short after its operator ran out of money.
summary: The Odyssey was intended to take guests around the world for years. The ship was seized in Singapore after its operator ran out of money, ending the voyage.
author: BBC World

title: Stay sharp, get used to loss – and pay your taxes: the wit and wisdom of Willie Nelson
content:
An exclusive extract from Willie Nelson’s memoir is paired with an interview that offers a glimpse into the country legend’s reflections on life and loss. The passage opens with a meditation on longevity, describing it as both a blessing—allowing him to watch grandchildren and great‑grandchildren grow—and a burden, as each day brings the death of another friend. Nelson notes that grieving can become a full‑time job and that the last person standing often feels lonely, emphasizing that loss is something one never truly gets over.

The narrative turns personal when Nelson recounts a moment when a friend’s wife died and the friend sought comfort from him. Nelson, who had already endured the death of his son Billy in 1991 at age 33, shared what he knows best: that while you do not get over loss, you can get through it. He concludes that the most he can offer is a song.
summary: An exclusive extract from his memoir • Read an interview with Willie Nelson here Longevity is a blessing and also a burden. A blessing because you get to hang around to see your grandkids and maybe even your great-grandkids.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Paul McCartney Named Billionaire, Third Richest Musician
content:
Forbes has reported that former Beatle Paul McCartney now has a net worth of $1.4 billion (£1.04 billion), making him a new member of the world’s billionaire club. The analysis ranks him as the third‑richest musician globally, behind Jay‑Z at $2.8 billion (£2.01 billion) and Taylor Swift at $2 billion (£1.49 billion).  

McCartney’s wealth is attributed to his extensive musical catalog, strategic legal moves, touring revenue, and an art collection. The bulk of his fortune comes from MPL Communications, the publishing company he founded in 1969, which manages his own catalog and those of other artists. The 84‑year‑old continues to build on this legacy.
summary: Paul McCartney's net worth is $1.4bn, making him the world's third richest musician after Jay‑Z and Taylor Swift. Forbes attributes his wealth to his musical catalog, legal maneuvers, tours, art collection, and his publishing company MPL Communications.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Cerebral Josh King plots unusual route into Tuchel’s England plans
content:
Josh King, the Fulham attacking midfielder, has drawn attention for his academic achievements alongside his footballing talent.  A product of Hampton School in south‑west London, he earned A or A* grades in all ten GCSE subjects and later studied A‑levels in French, maths and psychology part‑time, receiving grades of A, C and D.  He completed those exams in a hotel suite in Romania during the summer of last year while representing England at the European Under‑19 Championship.

King’s family background is equally noteworthy.  His mother, Michelle, is a university lecturer who is close to finishing a PhD in sickle cell disease.  His father, Steve, works as a lawyer, and King has said he might have considered following in his father’s footsteps had his football career not progressed as it has.

King is currently in the England squad for this week’s Nations League matches against Croatia and Spain, marking his continued rise into the national team’s plans under new manager Thomas Tuchel.
summary: Josh King, a Fulham attacking midfielder, is in the England squad for the Nations League matches against Croatia and Spain. He has an impressive academic record, having studied at Hampton School and completed A-levels while playing for England at the European Under‑19 Championship.
author: Guardian Sport

title: 13-Year-Old Leihani Zoric Aims for Olympic Gold, Inspired by Gilmore and Wright
content: The Indigenous Australian grew up idolising Steph Gilmore and Tyler Wright. Now she has them – and an Olympic gold – in her sights Leihani Zoric, 13, grew up watching Australian surfers dominate on the world stage. Stephanie Gilmore, the greatest female surfer of all time, and Tyler Wright, a two-time World Surf League champion, were among her idols. “When I was little I always watched their surfing,” she says. “They inspired me in and out of the water.”
summary: Leihani Zoric, a 13‑year‑old Indigenous Australian surfer, says she wants to dominate rather than just participate. She idolized Steph Gilmore and Tyler Wright and now aims for an Olympic gold medal.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Cricket Australia Declines to Reopen Ball Tampering Inquiry After Khawaja Book
content:
Cricket Australia has ruled out reopening the investigation into the 2018 ball‑tampering controversy.  The governing body said there is no compelling reason to open another inquiry, and Usman Khawaja has stated that the matter has never been about commercial gain.  

Khawaja’s book, released this week, reignited the controversy by alleging that more than the three players suspended had knowledge of the sandpaper plan.  

The three players—captain Steve Smith, vice‑captain David Warner and batter Cameron Bancroft—were handed long bans following a brief Cricket Australia investigation into the incident.
summary: Cricket Australia will not reopen the investigation into the 2018 ball tampering controversy that was reignited by Usman Khawaja’s book. The book alleged that more than the three players suspended—Steve Smith, David Warner, and Cameron Bancroft—had knowledge of the sandpaper plan, but the short Cricket Australia investigation had already handed long bans to those players.
author: Guardian Sport

title: England lose Immanuel Feyi‑Waboso and Tom Curry to injuries in Nations Championship
content:
England’s rugby squad has suffered a double blow ahead of the Nations Championship. Wing Immanuel Feyi‑Waboso sustained an ankle injury during the first half of the 45‑22 victory over Australia on Sunday and will miss the upcoming fixtures against Japan, New Zealand and the final‑week match against England.  

Tom Curry, who suffered a hip injury while training last week, is ruled out for the rest of November. The injury list also includes George Furbank, Ollie Chessum and Seb Atkinson, all of whom are expected to miss the clash with Japan on Saturday.  

With the squad pared down, the two‑try hero Henry Pollock is lined up for a rare start in the heavily altered XV.
summary: Immanuel Feyi‑Waboso suffered an ankle injury in the first half of England’s 45‑22 win over Australia and will miss the remaining matches against Japan, New Zealand and the finals weekend. Tom Curry sustained a hip injury while training last week and is also ruled out for the rest of November.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Trump Offers UFC CEO Dana White Press Secretary Role Amid Midterm Defeat
content: Trump has long relied on sports to project strength and fuel his culture wars. But after a crushing midterm defeat, even his UFC ally cannot distract from the political fallout In the wake of being destroyed in the midterm elections, it was only a matter of time before Donald Trump did something outrageous in an attempt to misdirect public attention away from his catastrophic losses. Before the midterms, published reports suggested the possibility of apocalypse, global or domestic – a nuclear strike on Iran, martial law to suspend last week’s elections, the invalidation of individual races, such as in Alaska – but Trump opted for banality over Armageddon, offering his vacant press secretary opening to Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO Dana White. It was absurd, and widely posited that a confused Trump had erroneously conflated UFC’s White with the Dana White who made more sense, former Heritage Foundation staffer Dana White. Because the public reactions made him look even more lost, confirming the sentiments of recklessness and disorder, utter chaos and buffoonery that led to the Republicans being routed in the midterm elections, the president said his offer to White was all a joke. As a disciple of the notorious McCarthyite Roy Cohn, who taught Trump one of his main political pillars – never apologize or admit wrongdoing. Ever. – Trump should not, of course, be taken at his word.
summary: After his crushing midterm defeat, Donald Trump offered the vacant press secretary position to UFC CEO Dana White, a move seen as an attempt to distract from his losses. Trump later said the offer was a joke, but critics view it as evidence of his recklessness and inability to admit wrongdoing.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Atletico target Zubimendi move - Tuesday's gossip
content: Atletico Madrid are reportedly targeting Arsenal midfielder Martin Zubimendi. Leeds United plan to step up contract talks with striker Dominic Calvert‑Lewin, while Barcelona are keen on Bayern Munich defender Jonathan Tah.
summary: Arsenal midfielder Martin Zubimendi is a target for Atletico Madrid, Leeds United plan to step up contract talks with striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin, Barcelona are keen on Bayern Munich defender Jonathan Tah, plus more.
author: BBC Sport

title: Wimborne Town to host Bradford City in FA Cup second round
content:
Wimborne Town, a seventh‑tier club, will host League One side Bradford City in the FA Cup’s second round.  
In the same round, former winners Leicester City will travel to face National League South side Dover Athletic.
summary: Seventh-tier Wimborne Town will host League One Bradford City in the second round of the FA Cup. Former winners Leicester City will visit National League South side Dover Athletic.
author: BBC Sport

title: FA, Team GB, England Netball Back Equal Sport Project to Lead UK Women’s Sport
content: The FA, Team GB and England Netball have joined forces to support the Equal Sport Project, a new initiative focused on advancing equality in sport. The project aims to position the United Kingdom as a global leader in women’s and girls’ sport.
summary: The FA, Team GB, and England Netball are backing the Equal Sport Project. The project aims to improve equality and position the UK as a world leader in women and girls' sport.
author: BBC Sport

title: Shapiro Promises Minimum Wage Increase and Abortion Rights in Pennsylvania
content: Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro (D) announced on Sunday that, after his party secured control of the state House and Senate, he will pursue a series of policy actions. Shapiro said he plans to more than double the state minimum wage, codify abortion rights in the state constitution, fund mass transit, and build additional housing.
summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) vowed to raise the state minimum wage and codify abortion rights into the state Constitution after his party secured control of the state House and Senate. He also announced plans to fund mass transit and build more housing.
author: The Hill

title: Senate votes 73-25 to advance bipartisan permitting reform bill
content: The Senate moved a bipartisan permitting‑reform bill forward on Monday, voting 73‑25 to advance the measure that would accelerate the construction of energy and other infrastructure projects. The vote clears a major hurdle, positioning the bill for likely Senate passage in the coming weeks. Senator Mike Rounds (S. D.) was the sole Republican to vote against the bill.
summary: The Senate voted Monday to advance a major bipartisan bill that aims to speed up the construction of energy and other infrastructure projects — clearing a key hurdle toward the measure becoming law. The vote was 73-25, teeing up likely Senate passage in the weeks ahead.
author: The Hill

title: Van Hollen in listening mode on leadership run
content: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D‑Md.) confirmed on Monday that he is “in listening mode” regarding a potential Senate majority‑leader position for the upcoming Congress. He reiterated that the selection should not be a coronation but rather a caucus discussion, emphasizing the need for a collaborative decision‑making process.
summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who has been recently discussed as a possible Senate majority leader for his party in the upcoming Congress, said Monday he is “in listening mode” on taking up the role.
author: The Hill

title: Trump Holds Surprise White House Briefing, Offers UFC Head Dana White Press Secretary Role
content: President Trump held a surprise press briefing at the White House on Monday, inviting UFC head Dana White, to whom he offered the position of press secretary. He delivered a combative response to the GOP’s midterm election loss.
summary: President Trump held a surprise press briefing at the White House on Monday. He teased reporters with an appearance by UFC head Dana White, offered him the role of press secretary, and responded combatively to the GOP's midterm election loss.
author: The Hill

title: Eli Crane Re-elected in Arizona’s 2nd Congressional District, Defeating Jonathan Nez
content: Decision Desk HQ projected that Republican Representative Eli Crane will win reelection in Arizona’s 2nd Congressional District, defeating Democrat Jonathan Nez for the second straight cycle. The contest was close enough that the projection was delayed until a week after the election, as Democrats prepare to take over the seat.
summary: Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.) is projected to win reelection in Arizona’s 2nd Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), defeating Democrat Jonathan Nez for the second consecutive election cycle.
author: The Hill

title: Cornyn Declines to State Vote for Paxton, Blames Corruption for Loss to Talarico
content: Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn (R‑Texas) declined to say Monday whether he voted for Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican who defeated him in the state’s Senate primary runoff. Cornyn said Paxton’s “corruption” was a major reason he lost to Democrat James Talarico.
summary: Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said he would not disclose whether he voted for Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. He said Paxton’s corruption was a major reason he lost to Democrat James Talarico after Paxton defeated Cornyn in a primary runoff earlier this year.
author: The Hill

title: Republicans Return to Washington After Midterm Losses
content: Republicans returned to Washington on Monday after an election rout that saw them lose both chambers of Congress during the final two years of President Trump’s presidency. Their mood mirrored their fortunes, with the blue wave prompting a GOP reckoning and raising questions about what went wrong.
summary: Republicans returned to Washington on Monday after an election rout that saw them lose both chambers of Congress during the final two years of President Trump's time in office. The blue wave forced a reckoning within the GOP, sparking questions about what went wrong.
author: The Hill

title: Stephen Miller Appointed as Trump's Chief of Staff
content: NPR’s Sacha Pfeiffer interviewed Chris Whipple, an expert on White House chiefs of staff who has written extensively about Susie Wiles. The conversation focused on President Trump’s appointment of Stephen Miller as chief of staff.
summary: NPR's Sacha Pfeiffer spoke with Chris Whipple about Trump's appointment of Stephen Miller. Whipple is an expert on White House chiefs of staff and has written extensively about Susie Wiles.
author: NPR Politics

title: France accuses Iranian military hackers of spoiling food at 700 retail sites
content: France has accused Iran of cyber sabotage, alleging that Iranian military hackers commandeered refrigeration controllers at roughly 700 retail sites last month. The hackers reportedly increased the temperatures during the night, causing millions of dollars’ worth of food to spoil.
summary: France says Iranian military hackers took control of refrigeration controllers at around 700 retail locations last month. The hackers raised temperatures overnight, spoiling millions of dollars worth of food.
author: NPR Politics

title: Carbon emissions from fossil fuels to flatline in 2026 as Iran war boosts renewables
content:
Scientists warn that talk of a global climate turnaround remains premature, despite a forecast that carbon dioxide emissions from oil, gas, and coal will flatline in 2026. This comprehensive assessment, to be presented at Cop31, indicates that soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged a shift away from fossil fuels.

The data suggests that emissions from burning oil alone will drop by 2% this year. This reduction is attributed to drivers economizing on fuel use and increasing adoption of electric vehicles, contributing to an overall easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions.
summary: Carbon emissions from fossil fuels to flatline in 2026 as Iran war boosts renewables.
author: Guardian Environment

title: AI predicts high cavity risk based on social determinants
content:
An international research team has applied artificial intelligence to identify individuals at high risk for cavities using data on social determinants of health rather than clinical diagnostics.  

The findings, published in the journal Caries Research, could help identify population clusters most at risk for tooth decay.
summary: An international team used artificial intelligence to predict who is at high risk for cavities. The study, published in Caries Research, identifies population clusters at risk for tooth decay using social determinants of health rather than individual clinical diagnostics.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Invasive procedures offer no long-term survival benefit for stable heart disease patients
content: An international study found that patients with stable heart disease and abnormal stress tests who undergo early invasive procedures do not enjoy longer survival than those who start treatment with medication and lifestyle changes alone. The research shows no long‑term survival benefit from routine invasive interventions.
summary: An international study shows that patients with stable heart disease and abnormal stress tests who undergo early invasive procedures do not live longer than those initially treated with drugs and lifestyle changes. The study indicates no long-term survival advantage for early invasive treatment.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Tai chi and matched exercise class improve sleep similarly in older men after cancer
content:
Tai chi and a matched exercise class both nudged sleep about equally in older men after cancer, according to a recent study.  

Sleep disturbances affect up to 60 % of people following primary cancer treatment and are often dismissed as a side‑effect of therapy or aging. For older men, scientific options are scarce, as most behavioral insomnia research has focused on women with breast cancer.
summary: A study found that Tai chi and a matched exercise class improved sleep similarly in older men after cancer. Sleep disturbances affect up to 60% of people after primary cancer treatment, and research on behavioral treatments has largely focused on women with breast cancer.
author: Medical Xpress

title: AI Analyzes Smartwatch ECGs to Detect Hidden Heart Pumping Dysfunction
content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) software that analyzes electrocardiogram (ECG) data collected by smartwatches may help detect a hidden and dangerous heart condition known as left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVSD). The preliminary, independent study presented today at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026 found that the AI’s ability to identify LVSD varied between smartwatch brands and across different ECG recordings.

The research was shared at the AHA meeting, which runs from November 6 to 9 in Chicago. The findings suggest that while smartwatch‑based AI could become a useful screening tool for LVSD, its effectiveness depends on the specific device and recording conditions.
summary: Artificial intelligence software evaluated ECG data from smartwatches to identify left ventricular systolic dysfunction, a hidden heart condition. Results varied between smartwatch brands and across ECG recordings, as presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago.
author: Medical Xpress

title: AI echocardiogram interpretations match human accuracy, cut cardiologist time by 50%
content: New independent preliminary late‑breaking science presented Monday at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago shows that AI‑generated interpretations of echocardiograms match the accuracy of preliminary reports prepared by sonographers and cardiologists. The AI assistance also reduces the time cardiologists spend on each scan by almost half.
summary: AI-generated echocardiogram interpretations match the accuracy of preliminary reports by sonographers and cardiologists, and the use of AI cuts cardiologists' interpretation time by nearly 50%. These findings were presented as independent, preliminary late-breaking science at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Childhood trauma associated with gambling harms in later life
content: A new study led by the University of Bristol reports that certain adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) raise the likelihood of developing problem gambling. The research, published in Addictive Behaviours Reports, found that childhood sexual abuse is linked to a two‑ to threefold higher risk of moderate gambling problems by young adulthood.
summary: Certain adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are associated with an increased risk of problem gambling, with childhood sexual abuse associated with a two- to threefold higher risk of moderate gambling problems by young adulthood, according to new University of Bristol-led research. The findings are published in Addictive Behaviours Reports.
author: Medical Xpress

title: YouTube Video Shows Pi and Leo Eating Raccoon Heart from Run-Over Roadkill
content: A YouTube video features two raw food enthusiasts, identified as Pi and Leo, consuming the heart of a run-over raccoon. The clip opens with the statement, "I'm Pi and this is Leo, and today we're going to eat some raw roadkill."
summary: The YouTube video features two raw food enthusiasts, Pi and Leo, eating the heart of a run-over raccoon. The video begins with Pi introducing Leo and announcing they will eat raw roadkill.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Researchers Discover Room‑Temperature Recrystallization of Molybdenum
content: Researchers from the University of Rochester and the Technion–Israel Institute of Technology have accidentally discovered a method to rearrange the internal structure of molybdenum at room temperature. Molybdenum, a metal that does not melt until it reaches more than 2,600 °C (4,712 °F), is commonly used to reinforce nuclear reactors, jet engine turbine blades and rocket nozzles. The new technique allows control of its atomic structure without extreme heat, potentially expanding its use to next‑generation semiconductors and other applications.
summary: Researchers Discover Room‑Temperature Recrystallization of Molybdenum.
author: Phys.org

title: Study finds Gatineau Park maple leaves show Cold War nuclear testing effects now gone
content:
Local scientists have maintained a continuous record of radiocarbon levels in sugar maple leaves from Gatineau Park for over six decades. A new study led by the André E. Lalonde National Facility for Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AEL-AMS) at the University of Ottawa reveals that the effects of Cold War-era nuclear weapons testing have only recently disappeared from the local biosphere.

The research, titled "Stored carbohydrates buffer Bomb and Suess radiocarbon effects in maple leaves across a 65-year Ottawa region record," was published in Scientific Reports. This analysis of the long-term leaf data highlights the lingering presence of radiocarbon from historical nuclear testing in the region.
summary: For more than six decades, local scientists have collected sugar maple leaves from Gatineau Park to measure their radiocarbon levels, creating the longest continuous record of its kind. Now, a study of those leaves led by the André E.

content: Walking through a farmers market, a parent carries a screaming toddler tucked under their arm in a “football style.” The parent feels tired and leaves the market without the produce they intended to buy, experiencing embarrassment over the situation.

title: Electrical technique concentrates milk without heat, challenging traditional preservation
content:
The headline notes that an electrical technique can concentrate milk without using heat, a method that would challenge conventional preservation practices.  

The accompanying text explains that the current standard for turning milk into powder is a highly energy‑intensive dehydration process that exposes the product to high temperatures. Powdered milk is widely used in the food industry because it can be stored and transported for long periods without refrigeration. However, the industrial method consumes a lot of energy and can alter heat‑sensitive components such as whey proteins, enzymes, and vitamins.
summary: An electrical technique concentrates milk without using heat, offering an alternative to traditional high‑temperature dehydration. Conventional powdering of milk is energy‑intensive, uses high temperatures that can damage heat‑sensitive components such as whey proteins, enzymes, and vitamins.

content: A KAIST‑led research team has characterized how light propagates through and is absorbed by barium titanate (BTO), a promising material for next‑generation optical communication devices. By clarifying optical properties that had been difficult to determine because of BTO’s complex internal structure, the study provides a foundation for designing these devices.
summary: A KAIST-led research team has characterized how light propagates through and is absorbed by barium titanate (BTO). The study clarifies optical properties that were difficult to determine due to the material's complex internal structure, providing a foundation for designing next‑generation optical communication devices.

title: Global CO2 emissions to fall in 2026 amid Iran energy shock
content: The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz led to a spike in oil prices Anna Ivanova/Alamy Carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels are expected to drop this year for the first time in five years. The slowdown has been partly attributed to the energy shock triggered by the US and Israel’s war on Iran. The conflict, which began in February, led to a jump in oil prices after the Strait of Hormuz, the main trade route for about 20 per cent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas, was blockaded by Iran in response. This is still affecting petrol prices and household gas bills, and has seen countries around the world turn to alternative fuel types to boost energy security. Advertisement Solar energy is going to power the world much sooner than you think Around 38.2 gigatonnes of CO2 are expected to be emitted in 2026 globally, according to the latest annual Global Carbon Budget – put together by more than 140 researchers. This is a 0.4 per cent decrease on the previous year, largely due to a projected 1.9 per cent fall in emissions from oil. The drop in oil use was partly offset by a 0.6 per cent increase in emissions from coal. Robbie Andrew at climate research group CICERO in Oslo, Norway, one of the report authors, says financial pressures due to the energy shock are likely to have caused the drop in emissions this year, which may turn out to be a “blip”. “On the assumption that there are no further crises, then you’d expect that emissions would bounce back,” says Andrew. The two biggest dips in emissions in the 21st century have been attributed to the covid-19 pandemic, which saw emissions drop by around 6 per cent in 2020, and the global financial crisis, which saw emissions drop around 2 per cent in 2009. The future outlook depends on how long the energy shock lasts, says Andrew, with governments forced to look at the economic case for continuing to subsidise fossil fuels. The rollout of renewable energy also played a part in bringing down carbon emissions. Electric vehicles and solar and wind power are predicted to offset 64 to 79 per cent of increasing emissions from demand growth through to 2028. Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter In China, the world’s biggest emitter of CO2, emissions are projected to decrease by 0.9 per cent in 2026 as the country continues to make strides with expanding renewable energy and electric vehicles. “What’s keeping emissions down is the renewable energy, and the price of oil actually suppresses this even more,” says Corinne Le Quéré at the University of East Anglia, UK, who also worked on the report. “So, that’s encouraging in a way, but it does mean that if the price of oil rebounds to pre-Iran [conflict] levels, most likely the emissions will rebound as well until we have enough further acceleration in renewable energy to really bring the emissions down durably.” Journal Reference: Nature Climate Change DOI: 10.1038/s41558-026-02821-8
summary: The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz led to a spike in oil prices Anna Ivanova/Alamy Carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels are expected to drop this year for the first time in five years. The slowdown has been partly attributed to the energy shock triggered by the US and Israel’s war on Iran.

content: A new UCLA study indicates that a naturally occurring molecule may aid breast cancer survivors in reducing persistent brain fog and fatigue. Researchers observed that women who took an oxaloacetate supplement for eight weeks reported marked improvements in memory, concentration, mental clarity, and overall fatigue.

title: Alzheimer's Early Warning Signs May Appear Outside the Brain
content: Scientists have discovered that early indicators of Alzheimer’s disease may originate outside the brain. In laboratory experiments using miniature systems built from human cells, researchers observed that genetic mutations linked to inherited Alzheimer’s can impair nerve‑to‑muscle connections without affecting the brain or spinal cord. This finding offers a possible explanation for why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems appear.
summary: Scientists discovered that genetic mutations linked to inherited Alzheimer's can disrupt nerve‑to‑muscle connections without involving the brain or spinal cord. This finding may explain early balance, walking, and coordination changes seen in patients before memory problems arise.

title: Perseverance Detects Chromium Luminescence Indicating Possible Rubies on Mars
content: Explore This Section Perseverance Home Mission Overview Rover Components Mars Rock Samples Where is Perseverance? Ingenuity Mars Helicopter Mission Updates Science Overview Objectives Instruments Highlights Exploration Goals News and Features Multimedia Perseverance Raw Images Images Videos Audio More Resources Mars Missions Mars Perseverance Rover Mars Curiosity Rover Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Mars Odyssey More Mars Missions Mars Home This heavily pitted, light-toned float rock “Nhlanguleni” was imaged by SHERLOC’s WATSON camera on Sol 2023, October 29, 2026, at “Kapama Karula” in the “South Idubi” region. NASA/JPL-Caltech Written by Roger C. Wiens, SuperCam Principal Investigator for NASA’s Perseverance rover at Purdue University Nov. 4, 2026 Exploration on Mars turns up the unexpected. Perseverance is equipped with a fantastic set of instruments for studying the rock record of this ancient planet. Both PIXL and SuperCam have great capabilities for detecting all kinds of elements. SHERLOC, SuperCam, and PIXL can detect minerals using various techniques including x-ray fluorescence, Raman, and infrared spectroscopies. As a side benefit of the way SuperCam performs its Raman spectroscopy, it can also study time-resolved luminescence. Normally luminescence occurs over a broad wavelength range (most of Earth’s commercial lighting uses luminescence in some way or another). Two years ago, the SuperCam team was startled to find strong, narrow luminescence peaks at two wavelengths of 692.7 and 694.1 nanometers when they shot a light-colored rock with the laser. This luminescence comes from delayed atomic transitions in chromium atoms present in a corundum mineral structure. SuperCam can time the delay of the atomic transitions via the resulting photons, and so we could verify that this emission came from chromium in corundum. The results were published in Geophysical Research Letters by a team led by Ann Ollila earlier this year, so you can read all about it. The gemstone version of chromium-containing corundum is ruby. Prior to installing SuperCam on Perseverance, we placed a ruby in the laser beam and watched the entire room pulse a brilliant red as SuperCam’s laser beam hit the gemstone; it was extremely bright. While we haven’t found collectable rubies on Mars yet, the little corundum crystals are helping us learn more about Mars’ past. Corundum is a metamorphic and pegmatitic mineral which we would not expect to find on Mars, a planet that lacks plate tectonics. However, large meteor and asteroid impacts can create local metamorphism due to long-term heating from the impact. Because we are in a very ancient terrain near the rim of Jezero crater, we can expect some evidence of localized metamorphism. As the first mission in such terrain, we are learning new things. Earlier in the mission we tried this technique only rarely; lately we have carried out the time-resolved luminescence observations frequently on light-toned rocks to look for more evidence of impact effects. It’s great to have this unexpected tool on board as we delve further into Mars’ deep past. Want to read more posts from the Perseverance team?
